title: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The distinct species inhabiting the separate islands of an archipelago are far more closely related to one another than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world, because the islands received immigrants from the same source or from each other.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: so that the inhabitants of each separate island, though mostly distinct, are related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland”. Scope: endemic species of oceanic archipelagos

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-13: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The closeness prediction is explicit and can be tested with phylogenetic clustering. Existing coverage is strong for well-studied archipelagos but insufficient for the full taxonomic scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure whether endemic species from different islands in each archipelago are phylogenetically closer to one another than to species elsewhere, using clade-specific trees and null models. Consistent within-archipelago clustering confirms the empirical prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Sequence coverage is sparse for many endemic invertebrates and plants.

Polyphyletic colonization can occur within an archipelago.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Monophyly, or shorter within-archipelago distances, is a standard phylogenetic criterion and matches the claim without much reinterpretation. Sequence archives and occurrence data support that test for many vertebrates and some plants, and leave most of the world's island endemics unplaced. The analysis itself is ordinary; assembling a taxonomically balanced sample is what pushes the work beyond a quick study.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within each oceanic archipelago, test whether endemic species on different islands are reciprocally closer, or form a single clade, relative to species from every other region. The claim is confirmed if within-archipelago phylogenetic distances are consistently the shortest, and refuted if closest relatives usually lie outside the archipelago.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many endemic invertebrates and plants have no sequences, so existing trees over-represent famous radiations.

Repeated colonizations of the same archipelago are a real biological alternative and require dense geographic sampling to detect.

Unsampled continental relatives can make an archipelago radiation look monophyletic when it is not.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For endemic vascular plants of oceanic archipelagos, the nearest relative on an independent synthetic phylogeny is, far more often than chance and in most cases, another species native to the same archipelago rather than a species from anywhere else.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Archipelago endemics were WCVP accepted species whose native records all fall in one of the 15 pre-registered archipelagos (4,746 species in 915 genera). All accepted species of those genera were matched exactly to Open Tree and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree was fetched for each genus (821 trees). For each endemic with at least one other archipelago native and one outside species in its genus tree (2,667 endemics), the first ancestral clade holding other tips was classified as inside (all same-archipelago natives), outside (none) or tie (mixed). The share inside among resolved outcomes was compared per archipelago with a null in which that clade's tips are drawn at random from the genus tree (10,000 simulations, seed 1); archipelagos with fewer than 10 resolved endemics were dropped.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: endemics of archipelago A = WCVP accepted non-hybrid species whose non-doubtful native records (introduced = 0) all lie in A. For every genus containing such an endemic, all WCVP accepted species of the genus are matched exactly to the Open Tree taxonomy (TNRS, context 'Land plants', no approximate matching) and the induced subtree of the Open Tree synthetic tree is fetched; tips are labelled A-native or non-A. A focal endemic qualifies if its genus tree has >= 1 other A-native tip and >= 1 non-A tip. Walking up from the focal tip to the first ancestor whose clade holds other tips, the outcome is 'inside' if those tips are all A-native, 'outside' if all non-A, 'tie' if mixed. f_in = inside / (inside + outside). Null per focal tip: the same clade size k drawn at random from the other tips of its genus tree (hypergeometric P_in, P_out); the null distribution of f_in is simulated (10,000 draws, seed 1). Archipelagos with < 10 resolved (inside + outside) endemics are dropped. SUPPORTS if pooled f_in >= 0.67 AND at least 75% of remaining archipelagos have f_in > 0.5 with simulated one-sided p < 0.05.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if pooled f_in <= 0.5, or if in a majority of remaining archipelagos f_in does not exceed its null expectation. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 5 remaining archipelagos: inconclusive (underpowered). WCVP or Open Tree API unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). The tie fraction (unresolved polytomies, often taxonomy-only placements) is reported.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: pooled fraction of archipelago endemics whose nearest clade on the Open Tree genus subtree is entirely native to the same archipelago (among resolved inside/outside outcomes)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: archipelagos with f_in > 0.5 and simulated p < 0.05: 5/8; with f_in <= null: 0/8

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'inhabitants of each separate island ... related in an incomparably closer degree to each other than to the inhabitants of any other part of the world' is read for endemic vascular plants: the nearest relative of an endemic should lie in the same archipelago. WCVP level-3 units are whole archipelagos, so 'separate islands' cannot be resolved except for the Mascarenes, which WCVP splits into Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues and which are pooled here as one archipelago (MAU+REU+ROD); for the others the test asks whether archipelago endemics cluster with archipelago natives. Relatives are searched within the genus only (genus trees from Open Tree), so endemics whose whole genus is confined to the archipelago contribute nothing. Archipelagos (WCVP level-3 codes): HAW, GAL, CNY, MDR, AZO, CVI, JNF, SCI, MRQ, FIJ, SAM, TUB, VAN, SEY, Mascarenes (MAU+REU+ROD); codes absent from WCVP are dropped. Plants only; Darwin's examples include birds and insects.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv

Open Tree of Life synthetic tree opentree16.1 via the v3 API: tnrs/match_names (context Land plants, exact) and tree_of_life/induced_subtree

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Where the tree resolves an endemic's nearest relatives, they lie in the same archipelago 69% of the time pooled (301 inside, 136 outside), against 14% expected from random clade membership, and every one of the 8 scored archipelagos is above its null (Hawaii 0.79, Samoa 0.87, Canaries 0.76, Mascarenes 0.62, Madeira 0.52). The pooled criterion (>= 0.67) is met, but only 5 of 8 archipelagos have f_in > 0.5 with p < 0.05 against the required 6: Fiji (0.50), the Society Islands (0.31) and the Marquesas (0.33) are significantly above null yet below one half, so the verdict is MIXED. Darwin's 'incomparably closer' holds strongly relative to chance, not as a near-universal rule.

84% of scored endemics (2,230 of 2,667) are ties: they sit in polytomies that mix archipelago and outside species, mostly because Open Tree places species that are in no input phylogeny as unresolved members of their genus. Results rest on the 437 resolved cases, which over-represent well-studied radiations.

Seven archipelagos had fewer than 10 resolved endemics and were dropped (Azores 7, Cape Verde 6, Galápagos 8, Juan Fernández 5, Seychelles 5, Tubuai 7, Vanuatu 3); Juan Fernández, Cape Verde and the Azores leaned outside.

WCVP level-3 units are whole archipelagos (except the Mascarenes, pooled from Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues), so the test asks whether endemics cluster with natives of the same archipelago, not whether species on separate islands are each other's relatives as Darwin's Galápagos examples did.

Relatives are searched within the genus only; endemics of island-endemic genera or of genera without other archipelago natives (about 2,000 species) could not be scored. Plants only; Darwin's evidence was mainly birds, insects and plants of the Galápagos.
